Chapter 7: Ceremony, Gratitude, and the Practice of Belonging.
There are those moments in life that really call for ceremony. I’m not talking about big, formal events, but the quieter rituals that mark our days—the way we notice the seasons changing, the times we gather with friends, or even just the simple act of giving thanks.
For a lot of us, ceremony might seem like something reserved for rare occasions. But if you live close to the land, you know it’s part of everyday life, woven into the smallest moments.
Picture this: a family stands at the edge of a lake, baskets in hand, ready to collect wild rice. But before they start, they pause. Someone sings a song. Someone else sprinkles tobacco on the water—a gesture of gratitude for the rice, the water, the sun overhead.
It’s such a simple ceremony, but it transforms everything. Suddenly, harvesting rice isn’t just a chore—it becomes a way of belonging. It’s a way of saying, “We’re here, and we’re thankful.”
Most people don’t realize just how much ceremony shapes the way we see the world. It’s not about following rules, or ticking boxes—it’s about paying attention. It’s about being present.
Ceremony invites us to slow down, to really notice what’s around us—to remember that we’re part of something much bigger.
Let me share another story. Imagine a group of friends gathering for a meal. Before anyone picks up a fork, they take just a moment to thank the plants and animals that made the meal possible. The words are plain, but the feeling? It’s real. And you know what? The food tastes different—richer, somehow more alive.
That’s when you realize gratitude isn’t just something you feel—it’s something you do. The more you practice it, the deeper it goes.
There’s also the memory of a child learning to plant corn. The planting isn’t rushed—it’s done with songs and prayers, with real care for the seeds and the earth. The child might not grasp every word, but still senses the meaning—in the rhythm, in the gentle touch, in the attention to every detail.
What that child learns over time is that ceremony isn’t about getting everything perfect. It’s about intention. It’s a way of showing respect, of leaving room for a little wonder.
In all its forms, ceremony becomes a way of belonging. It reminds us that we’re not separate from the world—we’re part of its ongoing story. It nudges us to give thanks, to care, to remember where we are and who we’re with.
In a world that often moves too fast and sometimes feels disconnected, ceremony gives us a way back—to gratitude, to relationship, to a sense of home.
